extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, mathematics educators, and students interested in the philosophy and pedagogy of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and qualitative standards for judging mathematical work: proof aesthetics, analog vs analytic solution methods, cognitive styles in mathematical thought, and the intellectual/educational values placed on different modes of mathematicizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic delight in proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof II exhibits a higher level of aesthetic delight than Proof I; many professional mathematicians would prefer Proof II.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons include brevity (after eliding formality) and that Proof II 'seems to reveal the heart of the matter' while Proof I 'conceals it' (e.g., starts with a false hypothesis and ends with contradiction). The aesthetic component is related to purer vision: proofs that reveal the core reason are judged more beautiful than heavy, plodding, or trick arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revealing the heart of the matter
rubrics_metrics.description: A desirable property of an argument is that it 'reveals the heart of the matter' rather than concealing it behind formal manipulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer proofs and solutions that make the essential idea transparent; avoid methods that obscure the underlying reason even if they are logically correct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: unconscious vs conscious mathematizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Unconscious mathematics: the mathematizing inherent in the universe and organisms (automatic, requires no brain or effort). Conscious mathematics: human, trained, symbolic, and often tied to tools (pencil, paper, instruments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize both modes: unconscious/analog processes operate in nature and organisms; conscious mathematics is cultivated and symbolically mediated. There is no sharp dividing line and both contribute to mathematical activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analog-experimental (analog) mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Analog mathematizing is sometimes easy, can be accomplished rapidly, may use few or no abstract symbols, and produces results often described as 'understanding', 'intuition', or 'feeling'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analog methods are accessible to many, suit spatial/kinesthetic reasoning, and can be highly effective for practical problems (e.g., building devices or direct measurement). They may nonetheless be difficult in some complex situations (machine parts, complex systems).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Analytic mathematics is dominated by symbolic material, is usually hard, time-consuming, fatiguing, requires special training, and often needs verification by the mathematical community to assure reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytic work is elitist and self-critical but its virtue is that while intuitions may be unverifiable, proofs can (in principle) be checked. Expect analytic approaches when rigorous verification and formal derivation are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: No a priori preference between analog and analytic methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither analog nor analytic methods are to be preferred a priori regarding accuracy or ease of performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If both solutions exist, agreement between them is highly desirable and can serve as a crucial experiment; real-world engineering typically uses analytic methods as starting points but fine-tunes to analog/empirical outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy of intellectual values — complexity/abstraction rewarded
rubrics_metrics.description: Intellectual acclaim tends to be proportional to the apparent complexity of abstract symbolization; what appears consciously more difficult is judged more praiseworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This hierarchy reflects practicing mathematicians' values; engineers or applied scientists may value functioning devices (analog solutions) more. Be aware of cultural bias: abstraction is rewarded in theory-oriented communities even if it lacks practical payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth of a theorem (deep vs trivial)
rubrics_metrics.description: A theorem is called 'deep' if its proof is difficult; elements contributing to depth include non-intuitiveness of statement or argument, novelty of ideas, and complexity or length of proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Trivial' is often a put-down but does not imply unimportance. There is an ongoing effort to simplify deep results; moving from analytic complexity toward more analog/transparent accounts is valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for simplification and alternative viewpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a constant effort towards simplification: finding alternative ways of looking at a matter which trivialize what is deep.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simpler, more revealing proofs are preferred when available; simplification increases understanding and aesthetic satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive style diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: People vary dramatically in primary modes of thinking (visual, auditory, kinesthetic, tactile); mathematicians commonly use visual or kinetic imagery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value and cultivate diverse cognitive styles; tolerance and recognition of different modalities of thought improve mathematical practice and education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical imagery and semiconscious thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical imagery is a semiconscious stream accompanying mathematizing; often analog, visual, sometimes musical, and can assist the dominant stream of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that nonverbal, image-based, or melodic thought can be integral to discovery and problem-solving; reflection can reveal a mixture of operations behind solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness of kinesthetic/visual proofs (example: Gomory’s theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analog/kinesthetic proofs (e.g., threading a labyrinth with a caterpillar chain) can make solutions transparent and give a powerful intuitive grasp.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, seek proofs that exploit visual or kinesthetic modes for accessibility and immediate understanding, even if an analytic formalization is later produced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of excessive analytical generality hiding intuition (Jordan Curve example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some statements are visually obvious (analog solution) but their full analytic generality makes formal proof very difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid introducing unnecessary generality when it obscures the intuitive content; consider parallel analog explanations to guide understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper goal of mathematical applications: automation/suppression into black boxes
rubrics_metrics.description: In applications, the aim is for the mathematics to become automated or suppressed — replaced by instruments, readouts, or programs so practitioners use analog surrogates rather than performing analytic calculations in real time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design applied systems so the analytic underlay is reliable but hidden from end users (e.g., astronauts responding to instruments), thereby enabling practical, rapid decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppression of the mathematical underlay in tools (example: computer art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Higher-level languages and interfaces can suppress the mathematical substructure so practitioners (artists, animators) can work without explicit mathematical knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When building tools, embed mathematical operations in accessible interfaces to broaden participation; this may make the mode of operation less analytic and more analog/linguistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defense of geometric/kinesthetic elements in education
rubrics_metrics.description: There has been a degradation of geometric and kinesthetic elements in mathematical instruction as symbolic/analytic elements prosper; this closing off of channels impoverishes mathematical experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve and develop spatial, visual, and kinesthetic aspects in teaching and research to use the brain's full capabilities; avoid overemphasizing only symbolic and analytic modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hemispheric complementarity in mathematical capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical thought uses talents of both cerebral hemispheres: left for language/analytic tasks and right for visual/spatial/holistic tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate contributions of both hemispheres; mathematical culture should encourage spatial and nonverbal modes as complements to analytic reasoning rather than suppressing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engineers' standard of success: functional realization
rubrics_metrics.description: From an engineer's point of view, an analytical solution is of little interest unless it leads to a functioning device corresponding to an analog solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In applied work value the translation from analytic design to reliable functioning artifact; practical success can vindicate mathematical elegance even if theoretical recognition lags.
